::: {.lead}
After launch day, the inbox of Byte Bay is full again: "I lost my phone and
my progress!", "The level pack downloads so slowly!", "Cars jump in the
races!", and one strange message: "Somebody wins every race in 3 seconds."
At the same time, the first cloud bill arrives, and it is twice as high as
planned. In lecture 21 you learned the cloud models. In this seminar you
**plan** the cloud of a real game: which services it needs, where they run,
how they stay safe, and what they cost. Every section ends with a task, and
at the end you have a one-page cloud plan for a mobile game.
:::

## Key terms

{{< glossary baas cloud-save leaderboard object-storage cdn dedicated-server cloud-region data-egress pay-as-you-go >}}

## 22.1 The services of an online game

An online game uses several cloud services at once (@fig-gamecloud).

::: {.callout-important title="Definition 22.1 — The cloud of a game"}
- **Back-end services (BaaS):** player accounts, **cloud saves**,
  **leaderboards**, often also friends, chat and purchases checks.
- **Object storage + CDN:** files that players download, such as level
  packs, art and videos.
- **Dedicated game servers:** run the live matches in regions near the
  players.
- **Analytics:** crashes, sessions and what players do.
:::

![The cloud services of Pocket Quest.](images/game-cloud.png){#fig-gamecloud width=94%}

::: {.callout-note title="Example 22.1 — Pocket Quest after the update"}
1. Login and cloud save through a game back-end service.
2. Level pack 3 (80 MB) in object storage, delivered by a CDN.
3. The live races on dedicated servers; the leaderboard in the back end.
4. Crash reports in analytics show which phones have problems.
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistake"}
Building everything yourself on a rented VM "because it is cheaper". For a
small studio, ready back-end services are usually faster, safer and
cheaper to run.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Do it · A map of services"}
Choose a mobile game you know with online features. Draw its cloud map:
which of the four kinds of services does it use, and for what?

*Your result:* a map with at least three services.
:::

## 22.2 Saves, files and downloads

Players expect their progress to be safe and their downloads to be fast
(@fig-save, @fig-cdn).

::: {.callout-important title="Definition 22.2 — Cloud save, object storage, CDN"}
- A **cloud save** stores a small file of each player's progress (a few KB)
  on a server, at checkpoints. After a login, any device can load it. When
  two devices disagree, the newest save wins, or the game asks the player.
- **Object storage** keeps files (objects) with a web address.
- A **CDN** keeps copies of these files on **edge servers** around the
  world: each player downloads from a near copy, which is faster and often
  cheaper.
:::

![Cloud save: the progress follows the player.](images/cloud-save.png){#fig-save width=94%}

![A CDN: copies of the files near the players.](images/cdn.png){#fig-cdn width=94%}

::: {.callout-note title="Example 22.2 — The lost phone"}
1. A player saves at level 12 with 840 coins; the cloud save stores it.
2. The phone is lost. On the new phone the player logs in with the same
   account.
3. The game loads level 12 and 840 coins. Without a cloud save, the progress
   would be gone.
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistake"}
Putting big level packs inside the app package. The download from the store
becomes huge, and every small change needs a new app version. Keep big,
changing content in object storage.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Do it · Find the cloud save"}
Open the settings of a game on your phone. Does it have a cloud save or an
account link? What happens to your progress if you change phone?

*Your result:* two short answers.
:::

## 22.3 Game servers, regions and safety

Live matches need servers that decide what happens, close to the players
(@fig-regions).

::: {.callout-important title="Definition 22.3 — Dedicated servers, regions, secrets"}
- A **dedicated game server** runs a match and decides what really happens.
  It is **authoritative**: a cheating phone cannot simply say "I won".
- Choose **regions** near most players: lower latency (lecture 19). Add
  regions only when many players live far away.
- **Secrets stay on the server.** Keys for payments or admin tools never go
  into the game app: anyone can unpack an app.
:::

![Latency from three cities to three regions (example values).](images/regions.png){#fig-regions width=94%}

::: {.callout-note title="Example 22.3 — The 3-second winner"}
1. In the first version, each phone sends "my race time" to the leaderboard.
2. A cheater changes the app and sends 3 seconds.
3. Fix: the race runs on a dedicated server, which measures the time itself
   and writes it to the leaderboard. The phone only sends its inputs.
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistake"}
Choosing the region by the lowest price only. A cheap region far from the
players gives every race 60 ms more latency.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Do it · Choose regions"}
Most players of a game live in Jordan and Saudi Arabia; 10 % live in
Germany. Use @fig-regions to choose the region for the races, and say
whether a second region is worth it.

*Your result:* a region and one sentence.
:::

## 22.4 What does it cost?

A cloud plan is not finished without a cost estimate (@fig-cost).

::: {.callout-important title="Definition 22.4 — A monthly cost estimate"}
List every service with its **use per month** and its **price** from the
provider's price page, and multiply. Often the biggest costs are **data
transfer out** (downloads, **egress**) and **server hours**, not storage.
Ways to save: a CDN, smaller files, servers only when players play
(auto-scaling), free tiers, and a budget alarm.
:::

![A monthly cost estimate with example prices.](images/cloud-cost.png){#fig-cost width=94%}

::: {.callout-note title="Example 22.4 — The bill that doubled"}
1. 50,000 players, half of them download the 80 MB pack: 2,000 GB.
2. Direct from storage at $0.09/GB: $180; through a CDN at $0.05/GB: $100.
3. 4 race servers for 24 hours a day: $288. Only 8 hours a day (16:00–24:00,
   when the players race): $96.
4. With the CDN and 8-hour servers, the month costs about $196 instead of
   $468 (example prices).
:::

{{< sim file="sims/cloud-cost.html" poster="sims/cloud-cost.png" title="Cloud Cost Planner: one month of Pocket Quest" height="760" >}}

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistake"}
Copying prices from an old blog post. Prices change and differ by region:
always use the provider's current price page, and write the date.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Do it · Your cloud plan"}
1. In **Cloud Cost Planner**, make a plan under $300 with the race region
   near the players.
2. Write a one-page cloud plan for Pocket Quest: the services, the region,
   the safety rule, and the monthly cost estimate.

*Your result:* a one-page plan.
:::

## Case study: Cloud Planner

The inbox of Byte Bay: a player who lost a phone, slow downloads in Amman,
jumping cars with a ping of 90 ms, impossible race times, a teammate who
wants to put a secret key in the app, and a bill that doubled because of
"data transfer out". The Game challenge of the interactive lesson uses
these messages. In the mini-game below you choose the service or the
setting that solves each one.

Unity Gaming Services documentation, "Cloud Save" and "Leaderboards"
(docs.unity.com). Glazer and Madhav, *Multiplayer Game Programming* (2015),
Chapter 13 (cloud hosting of dedicated servers).

## Exercises

1. Name the four kinds of cloud services of an online game.
2. What does a cloud save store, and when?
3. Why put level packs in object storage and not in the app?
4. What does a CDN do?
5. What does "authoritative server" mean?
6. Why choose a region near the players?
7. Where do secret keys belong?
8. What is egress, and why does it matter?
9. Name two ways to lower the cloud bill.
10. Why must a cost estimate say the date of the prices?

## Answers to the exercises

::: {.answers}
1. Back-end services (accounts, saves, leaderboards), object storage with a
   CDN, dedicated game servers, analytics.
2. A small file with the player's progress, at checkpoints.
3. The app stays small and the content can change without a new app version.
4. It keeps copies of files near the players, for faster downloads.
5. The server decides what really happens in a match, not the phones.
6. Lower latency for the races.
7. On the server (in the back end), never in the app.
8. Data sent from the cloud to the players; it is often the biggest cost.
9. For example a CDN, smaller files, auto-scaling, free tiers.
10. Prices change; the estimate is valid only for those prices.
:::
